processing: Sold as a green tea: spring leaf is fixed by heat, shaped and dried, with no oxidation. Exact steps vary between the many producers using the name.
harvest_season: Spring is the main picking, as with other Hubei green teas, and the earliest lots are the most prized.
appearance_dry: As is usual for Hubei spring greens, slender green twisted strands; the shape differs by producer.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear pale yellow-green, as with other spring green teas.
appearance_wet: Tender green buds and young leaves, as expected of a spring green tea.
taste_profile: Little specific tasting description exists; expect a fresh, fragrant spring green, as is typical of the class.

brewing.notes: Usual treatment for a Chinese spring green: a glass or porcelain cup, water well off the boil, and leave the lid off so the leaf does not stew.

vintage_note: Treated like other Chinese green teas: bought as the current spring harvest and drunk within the year. Check the picking date, since the name itself says nothing about the season. Nothing suggests it improves with age.
description:
Wudang Dao Cha, Wudang Daoist tea, is a regional name for green tea from around Shiyan in northwest Hubei, the city at the foot of Wudang Mountain. It is a geographical indication covering a whole district rather than one village's recipe: Zhuxi, Zhushan, Fang County, Yunxi and Danjiangkou are all named in it, along with Shiyan's own urban districts.

It is a green tea, so the essential work is stopping oxidation with heat and drying the leaf. Production details are not standardised in anything public, so treat each producer's tea as its own.

Good tasting notes for this name are scarce. Going by its class and region, expect a fragrant, fresh cup. Brew it the way you would any Chinese spring green, with cooler water and a short steep, because boiling water will flatten it fast.

Much of what is written about it is cultural branding: the Daoist link is the selling point. So buy it the way you would any green tea, by picking date and by how the leaf looks and smells, and do not pay extra for the word Dao alone.
history:
The name ties the tea to the Daoist temples of Wudang Mountain, and accounts of it lean on that link. How old the temple tradition of tea really is remains poorly documented, so the claims of great age are best read as local tradition. A 2016 news report described over a thousand mu of wild Taihe tea trees in the Wudang area, in Fang County and Danjiangkou, some of them over 200 years old.

The modern identity is more recent and easier to pin down. It carries geographical indication status, and in 2009 Hubei's provincial agriculture department called it the province's leading cultural famous tea, a title a national quality-products association extended to China in 2014.
